MSI SelectionTree, C++ Glass Wizard & MSI.DLL Dialogs

Every project compiled with BuildBootstrapper = true delivers two synchronized user-interface layers: the high-DPI GDI+ SetupWizard.exe external UI for interactive desktop installs, and a complete relational MSI.DLL Dialog SQL sequence inside Product.msi for direct enterprise msiexec /i runs.

Authentic Windows Installer SelectionTree

When a user selects Custom Setup or Maintenance -> Modify, SetupWizard.exe opens the embedded Product.msi read-only and renders an authentic Windows Installer SelectionTree with crisp 32-bit ARGB split-dropdown icons (zero 1-bit white/magenta halos in Dark Mode!):

  • Local Drive Icon: Will be installed on local hard drive.
  • Cascaded Dual-Drive Icon: Entire feature and all subfeatures will be installed locally.
  • Partial Drive Icon: Some subfeatures are selected while others are excluded.
  • On-Demand Badge (1): Feature will be installed when required (when AllowAdvertise = true).
  • Crimson X Icon: Entire feature will be unavailable (automatically blocked when DisallowAbsent = true).

Selecting any node updates the live Feature Details & Disk Cost card on the right and translates choices into exact ADDLOCAL, REMOVE, and ADVERTISE property lists passed to msi.dll.

Clean Live Progress Text (Zero Unexpanded [1] Placeholders)

instbuild.exe stores action descriptions (such as Copying new files) separately from ActionText.Template ([1]), and SetupWizard.exe formats every INSTALLMESSAGE_ACTIONDATA record through MsiFormatRecordW so users see real filenames instead of raw [1] placeholders.

Custom 370x270 MSI.DLL Dialogs

Need an extra configuration form inside Product.msi itself? Declare [MsiDialog.<Id>] and [MsiControl.<Id>] sections (or design them visually in View 8 of InstallerStudio.exe) to splice custom edit boxes, path pickers, radio groups, and checkboxes directly into the Dialog and ControlEvent SQL tables.

Outer Setup.exe Execution Level (asInvoker, highestAvailable, requireAdministrator) & UAC-Off Admin Checks (v0.5.1)

Starting in v0.5.1, authors can explicitly choose which Windows execution level instbuild.exe stamps into the outer Setup.exe Win32 RT_MANIFEST (#1) via [Package] RequestedExecutionLevel (in both .rsip manifests and the InstallerStudio.exe Application Information view): 

[Package]
Scope                   = machine
; Explicit Win32 RT_MANIFEST choice: asInvoker (default) | highestAvailable | requireAdministrator
RequestedExecutionLevel = asInvoker

1. asInvoker (Default — Just-in-Time Elevation When Clicking Install)

  • How it works: Outer Setup.exe starts with the caller's exact token, displays the Windows UAC shield on the Install button when Scope = machine, and elevates a single background --elevated-msi-worker broker only when the user clicks Install.
  • Advantages: Preserves the user's normal unelevated token when launching the app from the Finish screen (preventing Windows UIPI from blocking Explorer drag-and-drop and avoiding IT admin profile mix-ups on Over-the-Shoulder prompts), keeps mapped network drives (Y:\, Z:\) visible in Browse... pickers, and allows zero-prompt inspection or --help / --extract-msi runs.
  • Trade-offs: Prompts for UAC when clicking Install rather than at 0.0s launch.

2. highestAvailable (Elevate Up Front for Admins, Allow Standard Users to Open UI)

  • How it works: Stamps <requestedExecutionLevel level="highestAvailable" uiAccess="false"/> onto outer Setup.exe. Administrators receive the UAC prompt immediately at launch (0.0s), while Standard Users can still open the wizard without hard-blocking at launch (ideal for dual-scope installers that let non-admin users switch to per-user %LOCALAPPDATA% installation, or defer Over-the-Shoulder admin credentials until Install).

3. requireAdministrator (Immediate 0.0s Elevation Required at Launch)

  • How it works: Stamps <requestedExecutionLevel level="requireAdministrator" uiAccess="false"/> onto outer Setup.exe (displaying the blue-and-gold shield overlay on the .exe icon in File Explorer). Once approved at 0.0s, prerequisites and MsiInstallProductW execute directly in-process with zero mid-wizard interruptions.
  • Advantages: Ideal for "approve once up front & walk away" workflows, uninterrupted fullscreenblue / fullscreenteal 1995 retro washes, and custom wizard pages that inspect restricted HKLM or Windows Service state prior to installation.
  • Trade-offs: Standard users without admin credentials cannot open the wizard; mapped network drives are isolated from elevated tokens unless EnableLinkedConnections is enabled; and Finish-screen app launches require shell-token delegation (IShellDispatch2) on split-token Admin accounts so the launched app does not inherit elevated UIPI drag-and-drop restrictions.

4. Mandatory Administrator Rights Verification Even When UAC Is Disabled (EnableLUA = 0)

Relying solely on UAC's TokenElevation flag is unsafe on Windows workstations or servers where UAC has been turned off via Group Policy or Registry (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\EnableLUA = 0): when UAC is disabled, TokenIsElevated can report 0 even for real Administrators while requireAdministrator manifests and runas prompts no longer pop an elevation dialog for Standard Users!

In v0.5.1, SetupWizard.exe verifies actual NT security group membership via Win32 CheckTokenMembership(nullptr, BuiltinAdministratorsSid, &isAdmin) (DOMAIN_ALIAS_RID_ADMINS) alongside Product.msi Privileged LaunchCondition checks whenever Scope = machine (or RequestedExecutionLevel = requireAdministrator):

  • Administrator with UAC Off (EnableLUA = 0): CheckTokenMembership confirms active BUILTIN\Administrators membership and runs installation directly in-process without unnecessary runas loops.
  • Standard User with UAC Off (EnableLUA = 0): Because UAC is disabled and cannot prompt for elevation, SetupWizard.exe immediately blocks machine-wide installation with a clear, accessible "Administrator privileges are required to install this software for all users" dialog (and Product.msi enforces Privileged if invoked directly via msiexec.exe).
